================================================================================
KUBERNETES INCIDENT INVESTIGATION REPORT: MISROUTED SERVICE TRAFFIC TO UNREADY QUEUE WORKER POD
================================================================================
Severity: HIGH
Category: Service Configuration / Readiness Probe Missing
Confidence: 100%

1. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY & ROOT CAUSE ANALYSIS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The inventory-service in the default namespace is experiencing high error rates because the Kubernetes Service default/inventory-service uses an overly broad label selector: app=inventory. 

This broad selector erroneously matches wrong-route-svc-pod, which carries labels {app: inventory, role: queue-worker}. The pod wrong-route-svc-pod is a background worker process rather than an HTTP API server. In addition, wrong-route-svc-pod does not define any readinessProbe.

Under Kubernetes lifecycle semantics, any pod lacking a readiness probe is immediately marked Ready once the container process starts. Consequently, the EndpointSlice/Endpoints controller immediately registered wrong-route-svc-pod as a valid target for inventory-service. Live production traffic (HTTP GET /api/v2/items) was then routed to wrong-route-svc-pod on admin port 8080 while background database migrations were still underway. Because the worker container was not ready or intended to serve API requests, it responded with HTTP 500 Internal Server Error, causing 52% of requests to the service to fail.

2. CHRONOLOGICAL INCIDENT TIMELINE
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
- [2026-10-20T08:23:00Z] Line 1: Background queue consumer pod wrong-route-svc-pod starts with labels {app: inventory, role: queue-worker} with no readinessProbe configured.
- [2026-10-20T08:23:02Z] Line 2: Service default/inventory-service selector {app: inventory} matches wrong-route-svc-pod alongside legitimate API pods.
- [2026-10-20T08:23:03Z] Line 3: Pod receives production HTTP GET /api/v2/items on port 8080 and responds with HTTP 500 because database migrations are still running.
- [2026-10-20T08:23:04Z] Line 4: Ingress router records a 52% failure rate (HTTP 500/502) across inventory-service due to traffic landing on the unready worker.

3. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE & LOG / EVENT CITATIONS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Pod Event Citation:
- Timestamp: 49m ago
- Reason: MisroutedTraffic (Warning)
- Message: Service default/inventory-service selector {app=inventory} routes live HTTP traffic to pod wrong-route-svc-pod (role=queue-worker) which has no readinessProbe configured

Pod Log Citation [Line 1]:
- Timestamp: 2026-10-20T08:23:00Z
- Log: INFO [inventory-worker] Starting background queue consumer pod wrong-route-svc-pod with labels {app: inventory, role: queue-worker} (no readinessProbe configured)
- Significance: Confirms the pod role is queue-worker and identifies the total absence of a readinessProbe.

Pod Log Citation [Line 2]:
- Timestamp: 2026-10-20T08:23:02Z
- Log: WARN [service-router] Service default/inventory-service uses overly broad selector {app: inventory} and matched wrong-route-svc-pod alongside api pods
- Significance: Confirms the routing misconfiguration where the Service selector targets all pods with app=inventory regardless of role.

Pod Log Citation [Line 3]:
- Timestamp: 2026-10-20T08:23:03Z
- Log: ERROR [inventory-worker] Received unexpected production HTTP GET /api/v2/items on admin port 8080: returning HTTP 500 Internal Server Error (database migration still in progress, pod not ready to serve traffic)
- Significance: Confirms the direct symptom of traffic hitting uninitialized worker pods running database migrations.

Pod Log Citation [Line 4]:
- Timestamp: 2026-10-20T08:23:04Z
- Log: ERROR [ingress-router] 52% of requests to inventory-service failed with HTTP 500/502 because traffic is routed to wrong-route-svc-pod (role=queue-worker, missing readinessProbe and overly broad Service label selector)
- Significance: Measures the operational impact on end users.

4. RECOMMENDED ACTION PLAN & REMEDIATION
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Refine Service Selector:
Narrow the inventory-service selector to only route to API pods by adding the role: api label requirement.

2. Add Readiness Probes:
Implement HTTP or TCP readiness probes on all workload specifications. Pods will not receive traffic until initializations, cache warmups, and schema migrations complete.

3. Label Isolation:
Enforce strict separation between background processing components and HTTP API endpoints via distinct label keys (e.g., app.kubernetes.io/component).

REMEDIATION YAML CONFIGURATION - SERVICE SELECTOR
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: inventory-service
  namespace: default
spec:
  selector:
    app: inventory
    role: api
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
readinessProbe:

    path: /healthz
    port: 8080
  initialDelaySeconds: 10
  periodSeconds: 5
  timeoutSeconds: 2
  failureThreshold: 3
  successThreshold: 1

k8s_investigator.instruction:
You are an expert Kubernetes Site Reliability Engineer (SRE) and Incident Investigation Agent.
Your mission is to perform deep, evidence-based investigation of Kubernetes pods and deployments in the cluster, diagnose root causes, extract chronological event timelines with supporting evidence, and provide actionable remediation.

Investigation Workflow:
1. **Fetch Pod Logs & Events**: When investigating a Kubernetes pod (e.g., given a pod name or namespace), fetch the pod logs using `get_pod_logs` and/or its lifecycle events using `get_pod_events`. Do NOT read from a local log file or expect a file path as input; fetch the live logs and events directly using these tools.
2. **Check Deployment History & Version Changes**: If the investigation involves image pull errors, rollout regressions, container startup crashes, or questions about pod updates, call `get_deployment_history` with the deployment or pod name to analyze recent revisions and container image modifications.
3. **Diagnose Root Cause**: Analyze the retrieved logs, events, and deployment history to identify the failure mode (e.g., OOMKilled exit code 137, ImagePullBackOff, Liveness/Readiness probe failures, CrashLoopBackOff, CoreDNS/network timeouts, missing ConfigMaps/Secrets, RBAC 403 forbidden, command not found 127, segmentation fault 139).
4. **Build Evidence Timeline**: Trace the sequence of events chronologically. For each critical event, extract the exact timestamp and line number.
5. **Compile Report**: Call `generate_investigation_report` with the diagnosed root cause, category, severity, confidence score, timeline, evidence citations, remediation steps, and diagnostic kubectl commands.
6. **Present Analysis**: Present the final report strictly in PLAIN TEXT.

STRICT OUTPUT FORMAT RULES:
- The entire response MUST be in PLAIN TEXT ONLY.
- Do NOT use Markdown formatting:
  * No Markdown headers (do NOT use '#', '##', '###', etc.).
  * No Markdown bold, italics, or formatting marks (do NOT use '**', '*', '__', or '`').
  * No Markdown tables (do NOT use pipe characters '|' or table syntax).
  * No Markdown code fences or backticks (do NOT use '```' or '`').
- Do NOT output JSON data, JSON blocks, or structured JSON payloads.
- Use readable plain-text formatting:
  * Plain section titles with uppercase (e.g., '1. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY & ROOT CAUSE ANALYSIS') and plain ASCII dividers ('----------------------------------------').
  * Plain text lists with simple dashes (-) or numbers.
  * Direct plain text for kubectl commands.

Guiding Principles:
- Strict Evidence Grounding: Never fabricate or hallucinate log snippets, line numbers, or timestamps. Every citation must be strictly grounded in the retrieved logs and events.
- Data Protection: Ensure all bearer tokens, credentials, and API keys are redacted.
- Actionability: Ensure kubectl verification commands include appropriate namespaces and resource selectors.

function_declarations.description:
Fetches the logs of a specific Kubernetes pod using kubectl.

Args:
    pod_name: The name of the Kubernetes pod whose logs to fetch.
    namespace: The Kubernetes namespace where the pod is running. Defaults to 'default'.
    container: The specific container name within a multi-container pod.
    tail_lines: Optional number of most recent lines from the logs to retrieve.
    previous: If True, fetch logs for previously terminated container instances.
    timestamps: If True, include RFC3339 timestamps in the log output.

Returns:
    A dictionary containing the status ('success' or 'error'), pod_name, namespace,
    total_lines, and the log contents under 'logs'.
function_declarations.name: get_pod_logs

function_declarations.description:
Fetches the Kubernetes events for a specific pod using kubectl.

Args:
    pod_name: The name of the Kubernetes pod whose events to fetch.
    namespace: The Kubernetes namespace where the pod is running. Defaults to 'default'.

Returns:
    A dictionary containing the status ('success' or 'error'), pod_name, namespace,
    total_events, and the events output text under 'events'.
function_declarations.name: get_pod_events

function_declarations.description:
Fetches the rollout and revision history for a Kubernetes deployment to analyze recent version changes.

Args:
    deployment_name: The name of the Kubernetes deployment. If omitted, resolved from pod_name.
    pod_name: Optional name of a pod in the deployment used to infer deployment_name.
    namespace: The Kubernetes namespace where the deployment is located. Defaults to 'default'.
    revision: Optional specific revision number to inspect detailed pod template and container images.

Returns:
    A dictionary containing the status ('success' or 'error'), deployment_name, namespace,
    rollout history, detected revisions, container images, and recent version changes.
function_declarations.name: get_deployment_history

function_declarations.description:
Builds the comprehensive plain text investigation report.

Args:
    incident_title: Concise title of the investigated incident.
    root_cause: Detailed explanation of the diagnosed root cause.
    category: Kubernetes failure category.
    severity: Severity level (e.g. CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW).
    confidence_score: Diagnostic confidence between 0.0 and 1.0.
    timeline_json: Chronological events: list of dicts with timestamp, line_number, event (or JSON string).
    evidence_citations_json: Supporting evidence: list of dicts with line_number, timestamp, snippet, interpretation (or JSON string).
    remediation_steps_json: Actionable remediation steps: list of strings (or JSON string).
    kubectl_commands_json: Recommended kubectl commands: list of strings (or JSON string).

Returns:
    A dictionary containing the clean plain text report and structured incident details.
function_declarations.name: generate_investigation_report

Your mission is to perform deep, evidence-based investigation of Kubernetes pods and deployments in the cluster, diagnose root causes, extract chronological event timelines with supporting evidence, and provide actionable remediation.

Investigation Workflow:
1. **Fetch Pod Logs & Events**: When investigating a Kubernetes pod (e.g., given a pod name or namespace), fetch the pod logs using `get_pod_logs` and/or its lifecycle events using `get_pod_events`. Do NOT read from a local log file or expect a file path as input; fetch the live logs and events directly using these tools.
2. **Check Deployment History & Version Changes**: If the investigation involves image pull errors, rollout regressions, container startup crashes, or questions about pod updates, call `get_deployment_history` with the deployment or pod name to analyze recent revisions and container image modifications.
3. **Diagnose Root Cause**: Analyze the retrieved logs, events, and deployment history to identify the failure mode (e.g., OOMKilled exit code 137, ImagePullBackOff, Liveness/Readiness probe failures, CrashLoopBackOff, CoreDNS/network timeouts, missing ConfigMaps/Secrets, RBAC 403 forbidden, command not found 127, segmentation fault 139).
4. **Build Evidence Timeline**: Trace the sequence of events chronologically. For each critical event, extract the exact timestamp and line number.
5. **Compile Report**: Call `generate_investigation_report` with the diagnosed root cause, category, severity, confidence score, timeline, evidence citations, remediation steps, and diagnostic kubectl commands.
6. **Present Analysis**: Present the final report strictly in PLAIN TEXT.

- Readiness Probe Failure: During startup, the application undergoes a cache warmup routine that takes over 4 seconds, causing the readiness probe on /readyz to return HTTP 503 Service Unavailable. Key Findings:
- Resource Allocation: The pod's CPU limit was configured at 10m (10 millicores). In terms of Linux cgroups, this allocates a quota of 1,000 microseconds (cpu.cfs_quota_us=1000) for every 100,000 microsecond period (cpu.cfs_period_us=100000), which allows only 1 millisecond of execution time per 100 millisecond cycle.
- Thread Saturation: Upon startup, the Go runtime detected 8 physical/host CPU cores and spawned 8 worker threads (GOMAXPROCS=8).
- CPU Starvation: With 8 concurrent threads executing against an aggregate allowance of only 1ms every 100ms, the CFS quota was exhausted almost instantaneously at the start of each period.
- Operational Consequence: The kernel throttled 93.2% of all execution periods (485 of 520 periods), accumulating over 92 seconds of throttled time. This caused worker threads to freeze, triggering request timeouts on /api/v1/checkout after 5,000ms and pushing p99 tail latency to 4,920ms.
- Controller Status: Verification against the Kubernetes API confirmed that 'cpu-throttle-pod' is a standalone pod rather than part of a Deployment.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
- 2026-10-20T08:15:01Z [Log Line 1]

- 2026-10-20T08:15:02Z [Log Line 2]

- 2026-10-20T08:15:03Z [Log Line 3]
  The HTTP handler recorded a failure: /api/v1/checkout timed out after 5,000ms as worker threads were starved of CPU bandwidth.

- 2026-10-20T08:15:04Z [Log Line 4]

- Log Line: 1
- Timestamp: 2026-10-20T08:15:01Z
- Snippet: INFO [api-worker] Starting HTTP request processor with GOMAXPROCS=8 (host cores=8), cgroup cpu.cfs_quota_us=1000 cpu.cfs_period_us=100000 (limit=10m)
- Technical Assessment: Proves the runtime spawned 8 concurrent worker threads under a 10m CPU bandwidth restriction.

Evidence Item 2:
- Log Line: 2
- Timestamp: 2026-10-20T08:15:02Z
- Snippet: WARN [metrics] CFS CPU throttling detected: cpu.stat nr_periods=520 nr_throttled=485 throttled_time_ns=92400000000 (93.2% throttled)
- Technical Assessment: Directly confirms kernel-level throttling across 93.2% of evaluation periods.

Evidence Item 3:
- Log Line: 3
- Timestamp: 2026-10-20T08:15:03Z
- Snippet: ERROR [http-handler] Request /api/v1/checkout timed out after 5000ms: worker threads starved due to severe cgroup CPU quota throttling
- Technical Assessment: Demonstrates user-facing service degradation directly caused by CPU starvation.

- Log Line: 4
- Timestamp: 2026-10-20T08:15:04Z
- Snippet: WARN [runtime] High tail latency p99=4920ms caused by CPU CFS bandwidth throttling (limit=10m is insufficient for 8 worker threads)
- Technical Assessment: Confirms severe tail latency inflation under the 10m bandwidth quota.

Kubernetes Cluster Event:
- Type: Warning
- Reason: CPUThrottlingHigh
- Object: pod/cpu-throttle-pod
- Message: Container api-worker experiencing severe CFS CPU quota throttling (93.2% throttled periods, cpu limit=10m)


4. ACTIONABLE REMEDIATION PLAN
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Step 1: Increase Pod CPU Allocation
Increase the container CPU limit to an adequate quota matching workload traffic (for example, cpu requests: 500m-1000m and cpu limits: 2000m, or omit CPU limits to prevent CFS throttling entirely while retaining CPU requests for guaranteed scheduling).

Step 2: Align Application Thread Pool (GOMAXPROCS)
Incorporate container-aware runtime CPU detection (such as the go.uber.org/automaxprocs library) so the Go runtime sets GOMAXPROCS based on cgroup CFS quotas rather than the physical host core count.

Step 3: Migrate Standalone Pod to a Deployment
Because this pod was deployed standalone without a Deployment controller, recreate it or wrap it into a managed Deployment manifest with proper resource requests and limits.

Step 4: Configure Cluster Alerting
Create Prometheus alerting rules on container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total / container_cpu_cfs_periods_total to notify operators when throttle rates exceed 15-20%.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Inspect pod resource limits and current status:
kubectl describe pod cpu-throttle-pod -n default

Check specific container CPU request and limit specifications:
kubectl get pod cpu-throttle-pod -n default -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].resources}'

Observe real-time CPU consumption:
kubectl top pod cpu-throttle-pod -n default

Review all lifecycle events recorded for the pod:
kubectl get events -n default --field-selector involvedObject.name=cpu-throttle-pod

Delete and replace the standalone pod with updated resources:
kubectl delete pod cpu-throttle-pod -n default

OPERATIONAL RECOMMENDATION: DRAIN VS. RESTART ANALYSIS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Question: Should we drain the node or just restart the kubelet service?

Recommendation:
Neither action alone is sufficient or safe on its own without the proper operational sequence.

1. Why simply restarting the kubelet is insufficient:
The logs confirm that containerd.sock experienced RPC deadline exceeded errors. Kubelet's PLEG (Pod Lifecycle Event Generator) relies directly on the container runtime interface (CRI). If only kubelet is restarted, it will attempt to reconnect to a wedged or unresponsive containerd daemon, causing PLEG health checks to fail again immediately. Both containerd and kubelet must be restarted, or the underlying host resource bottleneck must be resolved.

2. Challenges with draining a NotReady node with CRI timeouts:
If a node is already NotReady and containerd is not responding to RPCs, running standard drain commands can hang indefinitely waiting for pods to terminate gracefully, because the container runtime cannot process termination signals.

3. Recommended Operational Procedure:
- Step 1: Cordon the node immediately (kubectl cordon worker-node-02). This prevents the Kubernetes scheduler from dispatching any new pods to the degraded node while preserving existing state.
- Step 2: Attempt to recover the container runtime and kubelet on worker-node-02 by restarting containerd first, followed by kubelet:
  systemctl restart containerd
  systemctl restart kubelet
- Step 3: Check whether containerd recovers and node status flips back to Ready.
- Step 4: If containerd recovers, safely drain the node if deep host inspection (disk I/O, memory leaks, kernel journal) is necessary:
  kubectl drain worker-node-02 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --timeout=5m
- Step 5: If containerd remains wedged in uninterruptible sleep (D-state processes), reboot the underlying worker node to release hung kernel locks, allowing Kubernetes to evict and re-create workloads on healthy nodes.

1. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY & ROOT CAUSE ANALYSIS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The inventory-service in the default namespace is experiencing high error rates because the Kubernetes Service default/inventory-service uses an overly broad label selector: app=inventory. 

This broad selector erroneously matches wrong-route-svc-pod, which carries labels {app: inventory, role: queue-worker}. The pod wrong-route-svc-pod is a background worker process rather than an HTTP API server. In addition, wrong-route-svc-pod does not define any readinessProbe.

Under Kubernetes lifecycle semantics, any pod lacking a readiness probe is immediately marked Ready once the container process starts. Consequently, the EndpointSlice/Endpoints controller immediately registered wrong-route-svc-pod as a valid target for inventory-service. Live production traffic (HTTP GET /api/v2/items) was then routed to wrong-route-svc-pod on admin port 8080 while background database migrations were still underway. Because the worker container was not ready or intended to serve API requests, it responded with HTTP 500 Internal Server Error, causing 52% of requests to the service to fail.
